title: Take nothing (Luke 9:1–17)
hook: the twelve sent out light, then five thousand fed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene and the women who paid for the road and stayed to the end. Your line was they ministered of their substance. Who did you thank? Day four hundred fifty-eight.

The charger, the spare charger, the snacks, the just-in-case jacket, the bag that won't close. That's packing for a weekend. Now take a mission instead: go to towns you've never seen, heal the sick, preach the kingdom of God. And the packing list comes back mostly crossed out. That's chapter nine of Luke. The twelve are sent out on their own. And when they come back, there's a hungry crowd of thousands and almost no food. Today, two scenes about having nothing.
screen: `THE BAG THAT WON'T CLOSE.` → `A PACKING LIST, CROSSED OUT.` → `TWO SCENES ABOUT HAVING NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Jesus gives the twelve power over devils and diseases, and then the list: "Take nothing for your journey; neither staff, nor scrip, nor bread, nor money; neither have two coats." A scrip is a traveler's bag, the kind you'd carry food in. No bag, no bread, no cash, no spare clothes. Stay in whatever house takes you in. If a town won't receive you, shake the dust off your feet and move on. Why so little? Luke doesn't say. One way to read it: traveling light means depending on others. The twelve have to knock on doors and be received. Their poverty makes room for someone else's welcome. And it works. Luke says they went through the towns preaching and healing everywhere. Then they come back, and Jesus takes them aside to a desert place near Bethsaida, and the crowds follow. Evening comes. The twelve make the practical suggestion: send them away to find food and lodging. Jesus answers: "Give you them to eat." They count what they have: five loaves and two fishes, and about five thousand men. And here Luke slows down. Jesus takes the bread, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives to the disciples to set before the crowd. Took, blessed, broke, gave. Catholics hear nearly the same movements at every Mass, in the words of the Last Supper. Everyone eats and is filled, and twelve baskets of fragments are gathered up, from what the twelve had called too little. The two scenes belong together. First the twelve learn to go out with nothing. Then they learn that what little they have, placed in his hands, is enough to feed a crowd.
screen: `NO STAFF, NO BAG, NO BREAD, NO MONEY.` · `TRAVELING LIGHT MAKES ROOM FOR WELCOME.` · `GIVE YOU THEM TO EAT.` · `TOOK, BLESSED, BROKE, GAVE.` · then, large: `TWELVE BASKETS LEFT OVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go through today lighter. Settle, and breathe. Picture what you're carrying into today. Not just in your bag. The grudge, the five worries, the backup plan for the backup plan. Pick one thing you can set down for the day. It might be literal: leave your phone in another room for an hour. It might be inside: one worry you hand over. Imagine setting it on a table and walking out the door without it. If you pray, you can place it in God's hands, like the five loaves. The bell holds the time.
Take nothing. Jesus' packing list for the twelve: no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, so they'd depend on welcome, and then learn that a little is enough. Today's word.
Your line: nothing for the journey. Today, leave one thing behind on purpose, and notice who or what fills the space. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the feeding of the five thousand from Luke on the solemnity of the Body and Blood of Christ in the year of Luke's Gospel, and some religious orders vowed to poverty take the mission of the twelve as part of their pattern of life.

fork.reveal: the twelve say send them away. Jesus says give you them to eat, blesses what they have, and twelve baskets are left over.

trapdoor: what you thought: take nothing means Christians should be careless about money.
what it means: on this mission the twelve travel light so they must depend on the welcome of others, and they learn a little is enough.
what a scholar hears: Luke gives the feeding the four Eucharistic verbs, took, blessed, broke, gave, which return nearly word for word at the Last Supper and at Emmaus.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens "Think about... Now imagine"; cut "for the first time"; the reason for traveling light is now offered as one reading, since Luke gives none; "toward Bethsaida to rest" corrected to Luke's desert place near Bethsaida; the four verbs are "nearly" those of the Last Supper (Luke 22:19 has gave thanks, not blessed) in teach, myth and trapdoor; cut the invented "one basket for each of the men"; "religious orders" softened.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 9:3 and 9:13.
